Ottawa. Question about an American reconnaissance plane missing in the Barents sea, north of the Soviet union, was raised in the House of Commons yesterday by H. W. Herridge, the ex-C.C.F. member for Kootenay West.
This misinformation has caused serious concern among some of my constituents and C.C.F. party supporters in the armed forces, who naturally wondered what had happened. This report is completely without foundation and is false. In order to establish the truth and to reassure C.C.F. supporters in the armed forces that the C.C.F. group in the House of Commons is a united platoon of men under the officer commanding, the hon. member for Assiniboia, I ask the minister to have an immediate correction sent to the troops by army signals, Toronto.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ACTION TO PROTECT OR EVACUATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Secretary of State for External


Affairs. Can he inform the house as to the situation in the Congo at the present time, and especially what plans are being made, or what action is being taken, either for the protection or the evacuation of Canadians resident there?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ACTION TO PROTECT OR EVACUATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian representative in the Congo is our trade commissioner, Mr. R. A. Bull, a son of Mr. W. F. Bull, our ambassador in Japan. He sent a message on July 8 and again on July 9 from the Canadian office in Leopoldville. I believe that most of the Canadians in Leopoldville have been able to get across the river to Brazzaville, in what was formerly the French Congo.
The situation in Leopoldville itself was reported in the message of July 9 as being under control and business going on as usual. Communications with other parts of the Congo are not, however, operating normally and we are not in a position to give a report as to the situation generally in the outer areas in so far as Canadian residents are concerned.
Our representatives in the Congo are coordinating their operations with those of their colleagues from the United Kingdom. Some time ago instructions had been given to the Canadians who had registered with our office in Leopoldville that in the event of trouble in their respective areas they were to try to make their way independently to the nearest British territory. We have not yet had any further details or reports as to what has happened outside of Leopoldville in so far as Canadian residents are concerned.

subtopic: ACTION TO PROTECT OR EVACUATE
speechtext: Is the United Kingdom government or the Canadian government making any moves toward evacuation of either United Kingdom or Canadian residents or citizens, or both?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ACTION TO PROTECT OR EVACUATE
speechtext: So far as I know no actual British planes are being flown into the area to remove British subjects. We are in contact with London in regard to this question, and whatever we can do will certainly be done.

subtopic: ACTION TO PROTECT OR EVACUATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we will naturally do everything possible in accordance with general policy to assist any Canadian residents there may be in the Congo.

Yes, my attention has been drawn to the article in question, and I should like to point out that again this is a general allegation without identification of the person who is said to have been improperly treated.
I think, therefore, that I can only repeat, and that I should repeat, what I have said on earlier occasions, namely that I have been concerned that in the handling of this investigation there should be no improper methods used by any of the police who are conducting it. I should like to emphasize that, and say the investigations which I have made satisfy me that the Hong Kong police as well as the R.C.M.P. are conducting their part of the inquiry in a proper manner, and that in no case have they abused their authority or treated persons other than strictly and properly in accordance with what is established by law.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON COMPULSORY PARTICIPATION IN EXERCISES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monieilh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: STATEMENT ON COMPULSORY PARTICIPATION IN EXERCISES
speechtext:
Last Thursday questions were addressed to me by the hon. member for Trinity and the hon. member for Essex East concerning regulations relating to civil defence exercises. There are no federal regulations or orders to compel participation in a civil defence exercise. Parliament has passed no legislation under which, in peacetime, such orders could be issued.
Civil defence exercises of the kind referred to are conducted by municipal or provincial authorities. Whether it would be within the power of the municipality by by-law or of a provincial government by regulation to make compulsory orders is a legal question on which it would be out of place to express an opinion here. Some provinces have civil defence legislation; Ontario does not.
The federal government as a matter of policy encourages provinces and municipalities to conduct realistic civil defence exercises. I think it is well to encourage public participation in such exercises as soon as those directing the exercises are ready to conduct them on this basis.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say very briefly that the special committee appointed for the purpose of reviewing the clauses of this bill has made its unanimous report, and I respectfully express my commendation of the committee for the harmony and identity of purpose that prevailed in its meetings in seeking to provide as good a bill as possible to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act and bring the benefits of the bill into effect as soon as possible.
Three amendments were introduced in the special committee, and as this is a bill that was preceded by a money resolution perhaps I might say for the record that these three amendments were introduced at my request. They come, of course, within the scope of the resolution that the house adopted prior to the introduction of the bill, and as we reach the clauses which are affected by the three amendments I shall ask one of my colleagues to move the amendment recommended in each case by the special committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as one of the members of the special committee I wish to say how pleased we were with the presentations made by the several groups that appeared before the committee. As a result of many meetings in a very short time, the committee presented a unanimous report with some amendments as suggested by the Minister of Finance, which are all to the good.
However, I wish to point out at this time that because of the fact that the bill is not retroactive, and the fact that the minister could not accept the suggestion that it should be at least retroactive to the date of its introduction in the house, it was not possible to consider in detail the many very valuable suggestions made by different groups which appeared before the committee. As one who is deeply interested in seeing the bill passed I would not want to be accused of causing any delay, and along with other members of the committee did not press at this time for a delay to consider any further amendments, which no doubt would have required considerable thought and time.
Nevertheless, I think the minister will agree with me and the other members of the committee that in view of the fair representations made in the many briefs from responsible organizations, which open up quite a field of study, it would be most desirable if the government would undertake to provide an opportunity at the next session of parliament for a similar committee to meet. I think it should be said that this was a very good committee, whose members worked together, and it probably presents a good case for having smaller committees. Those committees of which I have been a member whose numbers were limited to 10 or 12 members have always been the best type of committee and have done the best job. With a smaller committee it is easier for members to present their views and reach an understanding.
With that reservation in mind, namely that there are many aspects of the superannuation act requiring study which have nothing to do with the benefits granted by these amendments, I hope the government will agree that there are other very good amendments that need to be made to the act, and that as early as possible at the next session it will establish a small committee to study the suggestions which were made in the briefs and any further suggestions which may be brought forward.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if, this morning, we take time to consider certain amendments to the bill to amend the civil service super-


annuation act, I hope this will not be construed as a wish unduly to delay a bill which is of great interest to civil servants who will reach the age of retirement in the near future.
I fully approve the suggestion just made by the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) that the committee be reconvened next session, so as to give it an opportunity of introducing improvements as the need occurs and of making other suggestions to the government. After all, the representations made by the various spokesmen of the public service organizations contain a good many very interesting suggestions, which are worth considering. However, as it is important that this bill be passed immediately, we are unable at this advanced stage of the session, to study all those excellent suggestions in detail.
I know that the minister wants everything connected with the civil service superannuation act to be as up to date as possible. I believe that it would be an excellent thing to appoint a committee each year to study the suggestions that come up from time to time, for some of them could easily be acted upon, while others might not be readily acceptable.
For instance, there is a suggestion concerning women civil servants with dependents. I realize that a revision in this regard would have required so much work that the passing of the bill would have been delayed, and that the civil servants would not have been able immediately to benefit from the legislation. The proposal of granting to a married woman who is sole support of her husband and children, particularly when the husband is disabled, has much value. She is indeed in the same position as a husband who supports his family.
There are some other suggestions which might be considered but would be more difficult to accept. For instance, a widow on pension allowance who remarries should not be deprived of her pension. Some people say that the moral factor should be considered in the administration of this act. Anyway, the proposal has some value.
There are two other suggestions that are not quite clear in this bill. For instance, the loss of superannuation rights in the case of a person found guilty of an indictable offence. The legislation on this point should be clarified.
Some lawyers, including in particular, the chairman of the committee, told me that this was implied in the law. Someone with legal

training can easily read between the lines, but for a poor layman like myself, it is important that this chapter be made clearer, especially in the case of dismissal for cause. It should be understood that it applies to misbehaviour committed within the department and not outside. This is a most important point at present.
May I add that it would be very important to consider all proposals submitted, because they are all somewhat similar.
The main points are the same, and it can be seen, therefore, that the said bill still leaves room for improvement.
Therefore, if the committee were resumed to go into the bill more thoroughly and advise the minister, we might within a few years have an act second to none in the world, both with respect to clarity and to the possibilities it would offer.
The point I want to emphasize this year is that the bill should be made retroactive to June 20.
I know, as the minister has indicated, that if we make it retroactive to any particular date, there will always be someone who will be dissatisfied. I agree. One sure thing, however, is that it was on June 20 that civil servants were made aware of the government's positive intention to introduce those changes during this session.
The bill was introduced on June 20. Therefore, those who are on pension since June 20 have been much more hopeful than those who were to be pensioned off before June 20, because they now know about the benefits provided for in the bill.
I am sure that making the bill retroactive would not involve any considerable change from an actuarial point of view.
I think the mere fact of proclaiming this bill as retroactive to June 20 would satisfy those who have had to retire since that date.
Like the hon. member for Ottawa East, I therefore insist that consideration be given to those two demands: first, that the bill be retroactive to the date it was originally introduced in the house; second, that the committee be resumed next year to consider the other suggestions submitted by the various civil service organizations.

I welcome the fact that this bill is coming before the committee of the whole today so it can be considered and, after it is finally dealt with by this chamber, can be sent to the other place for their consideration with a view to having the bill enacted into law at the earliest practicable date.
As I understand the minister's remarks in presenting the bill to this committee for its consideration, his reference to the amendments which we made in our committee proceedings had to do with procedural matters only arising out of the fact that this bill, being a money bill, is preceded by a resolution, and therefore it is the better legal opinion that the amendments made in the special committee dealing with this bill require to be moved in committee of the whole by a minister of the crown. I take it that is the point to which he had reference there.
The bill really deals with one major point, namely changing the basis for computing superannuation by taking the base period as six years of employment rather than the former provision for ten years. That is the chief provision of the bill, and it is a desirable change. Many of the associations have recommended a change to a five-year period. The change to a six-year period comes very close to it, and it is a most desirable change. I think there is the desire to have that principle adopted as quickly as possible.
A great many other points were raised in the briefs of the associations. Some of them were extremely important points and some of them were smaller points. However, since each of those points affects some one person or other, I think we may correctly assume that each point is important.
The special committee gave each point such consideration as it was able, but because of the point we have reached in the session it became necessary to deal with the bill a little more quickly than might ordinarily have been the case, in order to assure that it would be back in the house to be dealt with today rather than risk delay that might put the whole matter of approval over until another session of parliament. I do hope that if that should be necessary the minister and the officials concerned with the administration of this act will continue to examine in a thorough
Public Service Superannuation Act way each of the points which were raised, because it seems to me each one by its own particular nature requires detailed consideration.
It is quite true that many of these points, while they appear simple, are not in fact simple at all, and that all factors involved in computing the superannuation dependent upon a particular recommendation involve quite a procedure and some of them do affect the actuarial soundness of the fund, which is something to be watched and guarded at all times.
Then there is the question of those civil servants who are already superannuated, and who because of special circumstances arising from when they were superannuated and the rates of pay they were drawing over the period for which their superannuation was computed, have suffered considerable hardship. I would very much like to discuss that whole matter, Mr. Chairman, but I take it the question cannot be discussed now since it was the subject matter of an act of parliament; therefore it would not be proper to deal with in on this bill, much as I would like to do so.
There is another matter of general application which causes me much concern. When you take a cut-off date for any changes in this legislation it always raises a problem, because there are some who retire immediately before that date and are therefore not entitled to the enlarged benefits of the new legislation, and consequently are in an unfortunate position. Therefore the matter of the date of the bill becoming effective as an act is of very real and special importance. I notice that this bill is to come into force on a day to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise a point or two on behalf of a few retired civil servants who retired on the basis of disability; in other words, civil servants who were forced because of ill health to retire on disability pensions. Some of them are very disabled. There are others who may be able to earn small sums during the working year, but for the most part they are disabled persons who must depend for their daily bread on the disability pension they receive.
Some hardship is being suffered by these people, and I should like to call the situation to the minister's attention in order that consideration may be given to relieving these cases. The amounts they receive are usually extremely small, because those concerned have had to retire early, let us say in their early fifties. They would probably not be receiving more than $3,000, and it is difficult for a family to meet all the bills which disability entails on so small an amount.
There is precedent for taking action. Since I became interested in this matter I have looked up the record in the United States, and I find that there a disabled civil servant has an income tax exemption to the extent of $1,200. In this country I believe there is complete exemption with regard to a former member of the armed forces. It may be that such a rule could be followed in the case of civil servants who have retired on disability pensions. The amount of tax money involved is so small that it would mean very little to the national revenue, but it would mean a tremendous amount to those who received the concession. It does not seem right to me that these people who find themselves in a difficult situation after having given the best part of their lives to the service of the government and the country should be taxed beyond their capacity to pay.
Whatever decision is made, I believe special consideration should be given to those who

have been disabled. Those of us who are able to work, or even in reasonably good health do not deserve too much consideration. However, I believe those who are unable to work should be properly taken care of under the superannuation act and I do not think that is the case at present. At least that is the information I have, on the basis of which I bring this matter to the minister's attention.

speechtext:
First, let me say
in general terms that I think all the points which have been raised in the course of the discussion, or which were raised in the four briefs which were presented by various associations and groups to the committee, were given careful consideration by the committee. I do not recall any point raised at the time which was not considered in the committee before it reached its conclusions and submitted its report to the house. I would not wish the impression to be left that there had been undue haste in the work performed by the committee. The committee worked very assiduously and diligently, and I think it carried out its task very thoroughly.
To dispose of one or two points before touching on what might be regarded as the principle point raised in the discussion this morning, perhaps I should refer first of all to the question of the position of dependents of married women who are civil servants. Let me dispose of this at once, because there was a very serious misapprehension in the first of the four briefs which were presented to the committee last week. It was in the brief submitted by the professional institute of the public service of Canada. The impression which underlay that submission was that children of married women employed in the public service had no pension status. That, of course, is entirely wrong, and I took the opportunity of pointing that out to the members of the committee. Section 13, subsection 6 of the act states in the clearest terms:
In this act, unless the context otherwise requires, "widow" includes "widower", but no person is entitled to an allowance under this act by virtue of his being the widower of the contributor.
For the purposes of this act and pension status under this act, the children of a married woman who is in the public service are in precisely the same position as the children of a man who is in the public service. The only difference is in relation to the husband of a woman who is in the public service. Her husband has not the status that the wife of a male civil servant has, or his widow on his decease. It has not commended itself to parliament at any time to make provision for the husband of a married woman who is employed in the public service,
Public Service Superannuation Act but as far as dependent children are concerned they are in precisely the same position whether it is their father or their mother who is employed in the public service.
The hon. member for St. Boniface raised questions about a particular case. I do not recall that he has brought that particular case to my attention, but if he does I will be glad to look into it. My impression from what I heard this morning would lead me to believe that the individual in question failed to make the election prescribed by law in the year 1953. Later another option was open to him, after the new legislation came into effect on January 1, 1954, which would have affected the basis of his payments. The law was there but evidently, as I understand the case, the man failed to comply with the law in the making of his election However, if the hon. member will bring the circumstances of the case to my attention I shall be glad to look into the matter thoroughly and appraise the status of the former civil servant concerned.
The next point which was raised concerns persons who are not now members of the civil service but who have been heretofore superannuated. The present measure has no application whatever to any persons who have been superannuated prior to the present day. I think the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam completely overlooked the provision which parliament made for them in 1958 and 1959. I put before the house in 1958 an item in the estimates to meet the exigencies of persons in this group, and that was adopted. Then in the 1959 session parliament enacted a statute to deal with the cases of such persons. That is the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act, and there was no criticism of that measure when it was introduced in 1959, nor was there criticism of the corresponding provision in the estimates introduced in 1958. I think I told the committee that a good many retired civil servants who received benefits under these provisions wrote in to express their satisfaction. I have heard very, very little criticism of that measure. It was one which was widely appreciated and which, I think, has served a useful purpose.
The final question concerns the date as of which the benefits provided by this bill are to take effect. The ordinary rule of this house is that statutes have effect from the day on which they receive royal assent. That is the standard rule if there is no provision in a measure to the contrary. We are dealing in this bill with a pension which is contributory. It is a benefit which is open to those who come within the definition of the public

Public Service Superannuation Act service in the measure and who contribute half the current contributions to the provision of the benefits. It is perfectly obvious that if the scale or the basis upon which the benefit is to be calculated is increased to the advantage of those to whom it applies, the date on which it becomes effective is a matter of concern to all persons who may be on the point of retirement. This subject was very carefully considered by the government and by the committee. I explained to the committee on two occasions the various stages of consideration through which this matter passed.
Obviously, if you attempt to date back the effect of the benefits of the bill to some earlier date than is normal, you are still going to find some persons who retired just before the date you choose and who will feel a sense of regret, disappointment and perhaps even discrimination. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, if you date back the benefits of this bill to a date before the increase in the payments provided by this bill, or the contributions in respect of male employees, then you are departing to that extent from the contributory principle.
It is true that this measure received its first reading in this house on June 20, but it was announced in the throne speech in January that amendments would be introduced to the Public Service Superannuation Act at the present session. And having regard to the fact that the basis on which the benefits are calculated has been a matter of discussion in this house over the years-I think I can recall discussions of a good many years; I believe the hon. member for Ottawa West will bear me out in that-I do not think there were very many civil servants who had not concluded that there would be a change in the basis of calculation, and that the effect of this would be to increase the benefits of those who would retire thereafter.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, there is in fact no reason for selecting June 20, or even any other earlier date, in preference to some other than the usual date. The fact is that if you chose June 20 as the effective date you would disappoint those who had retired on June 19, June 18, or June 17, and so on. If you choose any date at all, Mr. Chairman, you cannot escape the fact that you are going to disappoint some whose retirement occurred prior to the date selected. Therefore there is no escape whatever from that fact. In these circumstances, Mr. Chairman, it seemed to us that the only proper course to follow, the only fair course, on ultimate consideration is the normal course; that the measure shall come into effect on the date on which it receives royal assent.


The increased scale of contributions in the case of male contributors will become effective as soon as the regulations required under the act for the purpose can be promulgated. We may regret and express regret that it is not possible to extend this measure so far that no persons who retired just before the date that might be chosen would be disappointed, but we had to come back to this hard fact; that whatever date you chose there are persons who are going to be disappointed because they retired prior to that date. There is simply no escape from this problem, and it will always be so, Mr. Chairman, in connection with any legislation which increases the benefits for particular groups of persons.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think the committee of the whole is well aware that this matter was very carefully considered and did receive careful analysis in the committee. As to those persons who had retired previously, the other legislation to which I have referred makes provision for their cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Will the hon. member permit me? A point was raised by the hon. member for Ottawa West which I had intended to deal with but did not. He raised the question whether the increase proposed by the bill in the contributions by male employees of the public service exceeds in amount the cost of the benefits under the bill. The committee is aware of the fact that under the present legislation the contribution deducted from female employees is 5 per cent and that deducted from male employees is 6 per cent, and the government matches those contributions; so that the total contribution to the fund for every female employee today is 10 per cent of current salary and in the case of every male employee 12 per cent. The committee is aware of the report of the actuary, who reported that in his appraisal of the fund last summer he concluded that the cost to the fund of providing the existing benefits for female employees is 9.7 per cent, and the cost to the fund for providing the current benefits to male employees is 12.4 per cent. Therefore under the present scale there is an inadequacy in respect of male contributions. There is a slight difference between the contributions in respect of female employees and the benefits they receive, where the difference is between a total of 9.7 per cent in cost and 10 per cent in contribution.
We have here a bill which provides increased benefits, and the question raised by

the hon. member for Ottawa West in the committee and again in the house was whether the proposed increase in the case of male contributors is really needed for the purpose of providing benefits, or would there be some portion of it left over and above the cost of the increased benefits that might be used by the government for the purpose of reducing the existing actuarial deficiency in the fund.
This point was also raised in the submission made to the committee on behalf of the professional institute of the public service of Canada. Mr. Fletcher in his testimony undertook to challenge the calculations that had been made in the statement presented on behalf of the government. The following day the committee called Mr. E. E. Clarke, the actuary concerned. He is a senior actuary of the department of insurance. Mr. Clarke's testimony in this respect, I think, completely demolished the point that had been raised in the submission of Mr. Fletcher. Mr. Clarke was able to point out that Mr. Fletcher had not considered certain factors. His study of the problem and his calculations consequently were not complete. Mr. Clarke went further and indicated that on the basis of the experience of recent years it is likely that the cost of providing benefits on the increased scale, so far as male employees of the public service are concerned, may run up to something like 13.3 per cent.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think it correct to say in conclusion that the committee was given chapter and verse to justify completely the statement that this increase in the contribution by male contributors is required to provide the cost of the increased benefits for male persons in the public service. The bill does not contemplate any increase whatever in the contributions in respect of female employees. They will receive the increased benefits on the basis of their present contributions because, as I have indicated, their present contributions proved on analysis to be slightly greater than the cost of the benefits provided under the legislation in effect up until this time.
The increase in the case of male contributors is from 6 per cent to 6J per cent, which will be matched by the government. Accordingly the total contribution in respect of male employees now becomes 13 per cent.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there has been a lot of debate as to the effective date of the bill. I have no particular argument to present in that respect. I do not believe it matters very much whether the bill is made effective as of June 1, June 20, July 1 or even July 20. In my opinion that is a minor matter of detail. However, I think we have ignored one major
n, I960
Public Service Superannuation Act detail, the question of who will be eligible to receive the increased benefits being granted under the bill. The bill makes it very clear that the increased blessings will accrue only to those who are superannuated after the legislation becomes effective. I believe that the provisions of the bill, other legislation notwithstanding, should apply to all those on pension as a result of having been employed in the civil service. I see no reason why a letter carrier pensioned 20 years ago and living today should receive a smaller pension than a letter carrier who will retire later this year.
I know that even if what I now advocate, that the beneficial effects of the bill should apply to civil servants who retire in the future as well as those who have retired in the past, were given effect to, additional legislation would be necessary in order to restore equity. The minister referred in his remarks to additional and other legislation. However, I think, the bill now before us might help to a considerable extent in providing equitable treatment for retired civil servants.
I am concerned, as was the hon. member for Ottawa West, with the actuarial soundness of the public service superannuation fund, but I am even more concerned with the principle of equity. I can remember when a teachers' superannuation act was originally established in the province of Saskatchewan. Each employee agreed to the inclusion in the legislation of a provision providing for an additional levy upon himself in order that those members of the profession already retired would receive the same blessings and benefits as those then engaged in teaching hoped to receive at the time of their retirement. The same method was adopted in British Columbia when the first teachers' superannuation act was introduced; an additional assessment was assumed by members of the profession in order to provide adequately for those who had retired in the past.
I think there is much to be said for that, because our society is based more on moral values than actuarial statistics. Any society hoping to make progress must in the first place recognize its moral responsibility to those persons who have contributed to the public welfare in the years gone by. I hate to think of the fact that even at the time legislation was introduced in the house to provide pensions for members of parliament, members at that time were so selfish as to ignore those who had so faithfully served the people of Canada in the house in the past and were at that time no longer members of the house. I know a number of former members who have had to eke out a most meagre existence, while at the same time there are a number of young men no longer members of the house

Public Service Superannuation Act who are in receipt of retiring allowance benefits to the tune of $250 a month. One has only to compare the relatively young Ross Thatcher with the elderly William Irvine, the former member for Wetaskiwin-

Members of that parliament adopted exactly the same attitude that is now being shown with respect to the amendments to the Public Service Superannuation Act now under consideration. We conveniently ignore those who have already retired; then at some later date we decide that through additional legislation we will give them a little hand-out. In my opinion this is completely inadequate. Some measure of equity might have been restored if the bill now before us had included a provision that the additional benefits of this legislation would apply to those civil servants who will retire in the years to come and also to those who retired prior to this legislation taking effect.
It might well be that such a provision would require that the public treasury pay a supplementary amount of money into the superannuation fund. However, I feel there is a certain degree of immorality involved when we are willing to do something for civil servants who will retire in the years to come, and at the same time will not admit our obligations to those who have retired in the past.

Before we leave the bill I wish to reiterate that we would have liked very much to have these provisions made retroactive to June 20, because all those who were pensioned from that date onward were expecting a lot from this bill and they will now be extremely disappointed, even more than those whose pensions dated from the 17th, 18th, 19th or even the 16th. I really believe this would be a very small change to make, and it would help a lot of people who went on pension on that date.

Forestry Department

Title agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

the second reading of Bill No. C-82 respecting the department of forestry.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour for me to move second reading of the bill setting up the new department of forestry in the federal government. When the Prime Minister introduced the resolution he gave some of the outstanding economic reasons why the forest industry warranted the support of a full-time minister of the crown. If I may quote the words of the Prime Minister, he said there seemed to be good prospects for the Canadian paper industry to more than double its present production in 15 years.
This is a statement which should attract the attention of every Canadian interested in the growth and development of this country. It should attract the attention of every person in public life who wants to help provide new jobs for an expanding labour force. It should attract the attention of the agricultural industry because already there is a growing percentage of pulp provided by farmers from their farm wood lots.
If I may I should like to add a few figures to those provided by the Prime Minister, in order to impress on the house the significance to Canada of doubling exports from this, our most important export commodity. If I may have the unanimous consent of the house I should like to table for the use of the Hansard reporters a series of charts which I think can be reproduced in connection with my remarks today, and which would make the figures I am now about to give to the house a little more intelligible to people who read the report in Hansard.
