subtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR CREATION OF NEW DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the resolution preceding Bill C-82 respecting the department of forestry was passed, several hon. members expressed their views about the services society is entitled to receive from that new department.
I do not want, in any way, to repeat the arguments of my fellow members with regard to the importance of the lumber industry in this country.
The creation of a department of forestry is justified because of the importance but more particularly, because of the waste, of forest resources, not only in Canada, but in the whole world, as FAO pointed out during its convention last September.

Forestry Department
According to that organization, three trees out of five are cut down without being replaced. In Canada, we are no less guilty of waste even if the people seem to think that, because of our vast forests, the supply of wood is inexhaustible.
Other factors too help destroy forests; I mean insects and fires. Those are problems of concern to government authorities, both federal and provincial.
It is not too early to give some thought to the conservation of our forest resources, if we want to be in a position to meet the demand for wood products, a demand that will double within 15 years, and also to compete with Russia and other countries, but especially with Russia, which stops at nothing to get hold of our markets in the western world.
Mr. Speaker, the first thing that strikes me, when considering this bill, is the title: "Department of Forestry."
In my opinion, those two words psychologically imply an idea of authority which is causing a certain apprehension in the minds of provincial government leaders.
From a practical point of view, I believe it would have been better to name it the department of forest research, since the part the federal government is playing in the field of forestry does not concern forest management or administration, nor the control of cutting rights, etc.
The part of the federal government is well defined in subsection 5 of section 92 of the British North America Act, which reads as follows:
In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to-the management and sale of the public lands belonging to the province and of the timber and wood thereon.
This means that the part the federal government is called upon to play must be limited to research, preservation and use of forest resources, and not to management or administration.
This bill seems to go much further since paragraph A of section 6 says that the minister may take measures not only for the conduct of research relating to the protection of the forest resources of Canada, which is an excellent thing, but relating also to their management and utilization.
Several newspapers commented on this bill after it was announced by the government.
L'Action Catholique, of January 20, had this to say:
Under the guise of help, study and research, Ottawa is gradually penetrating into all fields.
And Le Droit said:
Will the federal government try to meddle with provincial affairs?

We have the Prime Minister's verbal assurance that this act will not encroach upon provincial rights. But if we can have as much faith in his words as in his election promises, we will be disappointed.
What I want to point out at this stage has to do with the small producers, that is the majority of farmers, woodsmen and people whose living depends on the lumber industry.
In a pamphlet published by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the number of people depending on the lumber industry is estimated at 361,300, not including farmers who have wood lots in addition to their farm proper. There are 35,000 of those producers in the province of Quebec and I do not think it would be an exaggeration to say that there must be about 100,000 in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, in the legislation and regulations that we will adopt regarding this department, we will have to give special consideration to the claims and requests made in certain circumstances by those workers.
At a time when farm income is steadily dropping it would be appropriate to include in this legislation regulations for the protection of those thousands of farmers whose sale of pulp wood or lumber represents added income, if not their chief income.
Recently, that is to say on June 7, 1960, we received a report on the value of the production of wood products for the year 1958. A study of that report indicates that the estimated value wood products production dropped by $17 million in 1958, as compared to 1957. That is a further reason for setting up this new department, which will be responsible for pushing production and finding new markets for our wood, both within and outside Canada.
Many Canadian farmers cannot make a profit out of their land, either because it is not fit for agriculture, or because they are settlers and their farm is not yet a going concern.
The efforts of the new department will doubtless be directed to the implementation of a research program for the protection, management and use of Canada's forest resources. However, it will have to stress the human and social aspects of the problem, that is to say the protection of the interests of farmers and tree farmers in our rural communities.
There is a need to integrate forestry to agriculture. Such a move would promote the

general welfare of the community. It would strengthen the economy of some areas on a permanent and stable basis, provided that some of the suggestions put forward by farm organizations and by the people concerned are included in the bill now before us.
I can think of no better way to summarize these suggestions than by quoting a statement made by J.-R. Pelletier, a former manager of the Ste Anne de la Pocatiere farm, when submitting a brief to the commission on land uses, on June 2 last. I quote two paragraphs from his statement:
(Text):
In regard to land use, we must consider, necessarily, forestry along with agriculture because both compete for the land, and it is my personal view that the two pillars of our future regional economy are, one 30 feet high, the tree, and the other one 30 centimetres high, the grass. As far as the Canadian forest industry is concerned the province of Quebec alone takes a slice of about 25 per cent.
(Translation):
I have no doubt that this proportion is the same in other provinces, particularly in the maritimes and Ontario.
A little further down, Mr. Pelletier went on to say:
(Text):
Again, I repeat that agriculture and forestry have to co-exist because we have nothing else to draw our subsistence from, and either one alone will be insufficient.
(Translation):
I could perhaps quote other arguments, but I shall refrain from doing so in order not to delay the passage of this bill.
As legislators, it is our urgent duty to pass sound and practical legislation so as to preserve that renewable wealth of our forests and to integrate it to agriculture in certain areas of our country.
Because the farmer has been placed in an untenable situation since the Conservative party came into office, as a result of the failure of its farm policy, we are inclined to think that it is introducing legislation on forest resources to make us forget that decline. However, we trust that this department will be more successful than the Department of Agriculture.
At this time when Canada is going through the worst unemployment crisis in its history, the launching of a reforestation campaign in our rural areas would be warranted as soon as possible.
This work would be a token of security for future generations and a qualifying certificate for legislators of today.
Recalling the final words of Mr. Pelletier in his brief, I say that the success of the task
Forestry Department
we are tackling will be judged by the importance of those taking part in it.
(Text):

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like to commend the government for introducing the bill to set up this new department. I realize there is a possibility of a conflict between this government and the provincial governments but, as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) stated in his opening remarks, the purpose of the department will be almost exclusively that of a research department. In examining the bill we find that clause 5 limits the authority of the department to that field over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction. Clause 5 reads as follows:
The duties, powers and functions of the minister extend to and include all matters over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction relating to the forest resources of Canada.
Clause 6 and its various subsections spell out more fully the powers and the duties of the minister. The people of my constituency, and this applies generally to the people of the province of New Brunswick, are vitally interested in the new department and its related subjects. As hon. members know, forestry and the products of the forest are of vital importance to the province of New Brunswick. At one time New Brunswick was primarily an agricultural province but recently there has been a decline in agricultural products and an increase in forest products. For instance, the net value of agricultural products in 1956, the last year for which figures are available, accounted for 11.2 per cent while forest products accounted for 14.3 per cent and fishing 2.6 per cent.
The total land area of my province expressed in square miles is slightly in excess of 27,000. Of this area 23,000 square miles are classed as forest land, of which 22,750 square miles are classed as productive forest land, so 80 per cent of the total area of the province is forest land. In a recent inventory completed by the department of lands and mines of the province of New Brunswick it was established that the forest area is increasing both in area and volume and that under ideal conditions of soil and climate existing in that province the forests showed a remarkable capacity for recovery. The inventory indicated that the total volume of wood in merchantable sizes is 16,900,000 cubic feet or roughtly the equivalent of 179 million cords of wood, of which 70 per cent would be softwood and 30 per cent hardwood trees. The last reported figures indicate that the pulp and paper industry in my province employed nearly 5,000 people with an annual

Forestry Department
payroll of nearly $20 million. One plant alone will spend nearly $8 million in the next two years on further expansion.
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) has set out very briefly and very well the historical development of the pulp and paper industry in Newfoundland and I think what he has said applies generally to the pulp and paper industry of New Brunswick. We have large plants at Dal-housie, Bathurst, Saint John and Edmundston. The plant at Dalhousie alone is capable of producing 900 tons of newsprint per day. In addition, and this was referred to by the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Stearns), we have a number of saw mills. Although the saw mills have declined in numbers, we have a corresponding increase in the pulp and paper mills. The saw mills employed nearly 3,000 people and, in the last year for which figures are available, paid approximately $5 million in wages. The combined selling value for the products of these two industries, the pulp and paper industry and the saw mill industry, approaches nearly $130 million per annum.
During the past few years, as a result of a change in the provincial regulations and a change in the basis of stumpage rates, the revenues accruing to the province from crown land reserves-I wish to say that the province of New Brunswick holds almost 40 per cent of the total forest area in that province -amounted to slightly in excess of $2 million, or slightly less than 50 per cent of the total revenues of the lands and forests department.
During the past few years great progress has been made in forest fire protection. I should like to compliment the minister on his presentation of this phase of the bill and suggest to him that there are great possibilities for development in the future. It is almost impossible to establish a trend in connection with forest fire losses, but it would seem that in 1959 the average was 17 per cent below that of the peak average of the 10 preceding years. The decrease in the number of fires can be traced directly to a better educational program and the development in the province of a forest ranger school, coupled to some extent with the influence of the forestry department of the University of New Brunswick.
I should like also to bring to the attention of the house the forest insect protection program which has been carried on in my province over the last few years. Since 1952 more than six million acres of forest land have been sprayed one or more times with d.d.t. at a cost of more than $12 million. In 1959 it appeared that this menace was over, but surveys in the fall of that year indicated that in certain sections of the province, there had

been a further outbreak and the spraying was resumed. The high mortality rate amongst the fish population and, to a more limited extent, amongst other species of wildlife as a result of the spraying caused the province of New Brunswick, in co-operation with the federal government, to modify the spray mixture to eliminate this danger while at the same time preserving the effectiveness of the spray for the purpose for which it was intended.
It is felt in my province that the establishment of the new department envisaged in the bill now under discussion will lead to a better understanding of the problems and preservation of the forest industry. I should like to point out that the conservation of the forest resources of New Brunswick is of vital importance to that province. I commend the government for bringing this bill forward at the present time to set up this new department.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. R. Granger (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
speechtext:
I welcome this opportunity of
speaking briefly on the bill which is before the house. I should like to say that I support the bill because it gives to the woods industry, I believe, its proper place in the Canadian economy. In my own province of Newfoundland the woods industry is very important, even as it is important to the whole Canadian economy. This statement applies particularly to my district of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, for in that district there is not only one of the largest paper mills in the world but also many of the men who do the work which keeps the mills at Grand Falls and the other paper mills in Newfoundland operating reside there.
Perhaps nothing illustrates more graphically the importance of the woods industry in Newfoundland than an enumeration of the towns which depend upon it. First, I might mention Grand Falls itself, where the Anglo-Newfoundland Development Company's paper mill was built in 1905. Next to Grand Falls is the town of Windsor; then Bishop's Falls, Glenwood, Badger and Millertown, as well as other places which depend on the industrial side of the manufacturing of pulp and paper. Then there is the port of Botwood, which is an important shipping centre, through which the paper is shipped. There are many other communities which I will not take the time to mention, White Bay and Green Bay, where the people find at least part of their year's employment in the cutting of wood. I think, too, of the new towns such as Springdale, Robert's Arm and King's Point, which have grown up as a result of the pulp and paper industry. This industry, while it does not employ as many people or affect as many people directly as the fisheries in Newfoundland, nevertheless its dollar value is greater

than that of any other industry. It follows, therefore, that this industry is of vital importance to the province of Newfoundland. The creation of the department of forestry is a move which will be welcomed by those who are interested in the development of the woods industry.
Apart from Newfoundland itself, the timber resources of Labrador are practically untouched and are vast. I would hope, in the future, to see the development of these great resources. I might add that we have already two great pulp and paper mills in Newfoundland and if the consistent and energetic efforts of Premier Smallwood bear fruit, we will have a third. Certainly we do have vast timber resources.
I was particularly impressed with the remarks which the minister made in connection with fire fighting. Forest fires have been the historic enemy of the woods industry. From time to time we have had some very serious fires in Newfoundland. Last year there was a bad one in Labrador and other serious fires in the Baie Verte area. Although the provincial department of mines and resources and the companies themselves have made exhaustive efforts to combat the forest fires, they do occur. I should like to associate myself with the remarks made by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) when he mentioned the work that has been done in protecting and conserving the forests. Nevertheless, when it comes to research, only the federal government can do a satisfactory and complete job, even as in fisheries where research and development is done by a federal body.
Not only are the forests of Newfoundland important now but as far as we can see in the future the forests will continue to be important and will be absolutely vital to the economic well-being of Newfoundland and Labrador. If these forests are to continue to provide necessary employment, if they are to continue to be of use to future generations, it is now that conservation measures must be studied; it is now that research must be conducted, and it is now that the work must be done to protect the future of the industry and ensure its progress.
In passing and speaking of work which has already been done I should like to suggest that even at this late date the federal government might consider making payment retroactively for the work which has been done in forestry research and protection in Newfoundland.
I should also like to mention in passing one thing which is related to this matter, namely the port of Botwood which is the shipping port for pulp and paper from central
Forestry Department
Newfoundland. It may very well, as a result of the services provided now by icebreakers, become an all year round shipping port to the great benefit of the people who are living there whereas in the past quite frequently other ports had to be used for the shipping of pulp.
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's put forward several suggestions with which I should like to associate myself. One was with regard to research dealing with the present use of wood and the possibility of new uses. I think that matter is particularly important because there is a certain amount of waste. If all the wood could be used industrially that fact in itself would be a kind of conservation, and one which would be profitable.
The hon. member mentioned trading policies. As is well known, Canadian exporters suffer from extremely keen competition. I would say that our exports, although increasing, have not increased as fast as have those of our competitors. I think the new department of forestry should look carefully into the possibility of improving our export position. The hon. member for Humber-St. George's mentioned co-operation between the industry, provincial governments and the federal government with regard to scientific forest development. That suggestion I heartily endorse and I imagine it will follow. He also mentioned security of land tenure and study of the position of the forest industries within the Canadian tax structure. These things which were mentioned by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's I hope will be given serious consideration by the new department.
With respect to the development of the forest resources of Labrador may I say I would hope that these are not overlooked by the new department and also in connection with northern development. There we have great natural resources. They are probably among the greatest untapped resources in the world. The new department will have boundless opportunities of looking into the development of our woods resources and in that endeavour I wish them the very best of success because the woods industry in Canada is one of our top industries, and in our own province of Newfoundland, as I stated previously, it is of terrific value.
To come back again to my own particular part of the province of Newfoundland, namely the district of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, may I say that the woods industry affects so many people in so many ways that it is absolutely essential, first, that it be conserved; second, that it be enlarged; and, third, initiating in Canada as a whole, that the development of these resources be such that

Forestry Department
more and more Newfoundlanders and more and more Canadians in every part of Canada may be able to make a living from our great Canadian forests.

Mr. Speaker, I should first like to congratulate this government upon the proposal to establish a federal department of forestry and on recognizing the importance of the forest industry to the economy and welfare of Canada. In British Columbia the forest industries support approximately 60 per cent of the economy of the province, directly or indirectly. I feel that we have in my own province a very efficient forestry department which is manned by a capable and efficient staff of experienced foresters. I believe this new department can work efficiently and effectively with the provincial departments and do a great service in the fields of research, conservation and reforestation. It should also take on a considerable share of the responsibilities of fire protection and fire Bghting in co-operation with the provincial departments.
I would also hope that this department would take a keen interest in sales promotion of the products of the forest, especially British Columbia lumber and plywood in the United Kingdom market. The per capita consumption of timber in Britain today is one of the lowest among industrial nations. I believe that in co-operation with the British Columbia government, the British Columbia lumber manufacturers association and the export sales organizations, we could promote the use of Canadian standard dressing, making it possible to ship specific parcels as to size, length and grade, thereby reducing considerably the cost of shipping, handling and sorting and putting Canada into a position to compete with Russia and the Baltic states. I also believe that we should promote in Great Britain the use of standard frame construction with brick veneer exteriors, something which would also reduce construction costs and bring back the per capita consumption of timber in the United Kingdom to something like pre-war levels.
We in British Columbia are faced with terrific competition from Russia. I should like to say a few words with regard to that matter and with regard to Russian selling tactics. I do not think anyone can accuse them of outright dumping. Their methods are much more subtle than that. What the Russians do is to incorporate a rebate. For example, they open their 1960 selling campaign in December, 1959 and come out with a price that is at that time just sufficiently under the going market price to assure acceptance. Then on subsequent offerings at
fMr. Granger.]
price reductions, they offer to reduce the price of previous purchases, depending on the amount of new purchasing which the importer does. In other words, no importer can afford not to buy from the Russians because he is being assured of a rebate on his previous purchases.
To me this is a vicious kind of commercial blackmail with which no commercial company can compete. I am sure the people of British Columbia who are interested in the forest industry and those who are working in the mills and in the logging camps would greatly appreciate anything this government can do to bring back the great British market for British Columbia lumber.
May I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks are going to be very brief. I wish only to register my own enthusiastic approval of this proposed legislation. I happen to represent a constituency the economy of which depends to a large degree on forests and forest products. The pulp and paper industry is one of the major employers of labour in our district, and therefore I am heartily in favour of this bill and its objectives, including research, good management and utilization and, as pointed out by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), the importance of obtaining in co-operation with the provinces a greater measure of fire protection.
The forest industry, which alone of the great national basic industries receives no subsidy and is not seeking any, when compared with annual production from agriculture or mining pays out the most wages, produces a greater total buying power, contributes vastly more to a favourable trade balance, supports the greatest export trade, and produces the largest tax revenue if we combine taxes levied by both the provincial and federal governments.
Our federal government spends approximately each year $6 million on forest administration and research. It spends $25 million on mining administration, research and subsidy. It spends $18 million on agriculture administration research and subsidy. What are the revenues from these basic industries? Federal and provincial governments receive $230 million in revenue annually from agriculture on which they spend $150 million. From the forests these two senior governments

receive $275 million on which they spend a combined total of only $45 million. Mr. Speaker, from these figures it can be seen that we can afford to be a little more generous toward a basic industry for which we should be very thankful.
In our district of Thunder bay we have a great number of small farmers dependent for the most part for their livelihood upon wood losts. I express the hope that this new minister of forestry will take into account the W'elfare of these farmers by rendering some form of assistance in marketing their wood and will also explore the possibilities for improved production, improved management and technique, et cetera. The possibilities of developing local non-farm industry, and by that I mean industry relating to farming and forestry, should be carefully investigated in the interests of bettering rural community life by stabilizing population which an aggressive federal department of forestry may well undertake and bring about a new era for the wood lot farmer of our district and other districts in Canada.
An economic survey of northwestern Ontario issued by the Ontario department of economics contains some very interesting data concerning the income of pulp and paper workers, which is shown as being about $700 above the average industrial worker per year. I am not going to quote statistics; I merely wish to emphasize the importance of this industry and to say how glad I am that this new forestry department is at least being established.
The forests of Thunder bay have built the towns of Red Rock, Terrace Bay, Nipigon, Longlac and Marathon. Incidentally, although I say that, these towns are within the constituency of my friend, the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). There should be no need to stress the importance of the pulp and paper and lumber industry to the well-being of Canada. This is generally recognized. It is there for everyone to see and it is satisfying to know that from Newfoundland to British Columbia this move to establish a new forestry department has been hailed as a progressive step toward a better management of our forests and effective coordination of federal and provincial responsibilities for the advancement of a truly Canadian forest policy. This policy should encourage an expansion in the field of forest products research which we all hope the passing of this bill will provide.
Forestry Department
The unanimity of approval of this bill augurs well for the success of the measure and I congratulate the minister. All that remains now is for the appointment of a minister whose training and temperament I hope may not be too far removed from that of a good woodsman.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, forests and water power are two interdependent and mutually sustaining resources. Our forests are of primary importance in the Canadian economy, since they cover 46 per cent of Canada's territory. They contain 170 different species of trees, 55 of which are of commercial use, 23 of the evergreen or softwood varieties and 32 of the deciduous or hardwood varieties.
Our forests are a substantial source of wealth, giving rise to many primary and secondary industries. They protect our water resources, safeguard the fertility of our soil and help check erosion. They promote our tourist industry and help improve our trade balance.
We must protect our forests, first against fire; second, against indiscriminate lumbering; third, against diseases and insect pests such as the spruce budworm, and I strongly urge the new department to extend research in order, first to control diseases and, second, to discover new uses for waste wood-products.
I strongly urge the government to add to this department a credit fund to enable farmers to improve their wood lots, by means of restocking, etc.
I think that a forest credit such as this would be of tremendous help for all the farmers in this country who have wood lots.
Since forest and soil are interdependent, it would be appropriate to appoint an agronomist as deputy minister.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to take part briefly in the debate on the establishment of a federal department of forestry.
The forests of our country and of my province in particular are a very important asset to the general economy. Forests actually cover 40 per cent of Canada and almost 80 per cent of the province of Quebec.
In my own area, commonly referred to as the "blueberry area", forestry is an important source of revenue. It is almost a regional heritage.

Forestry Department
Several companies have mills there, Consolidated Paper, Price Brothers Limited, and the Lake St. John mill, in Dolbeau, in Ro-berval riding.
Forestry therefore, plays a foremost part not only in the economy of my area but in the economy of the province of Quebec in general and of the whole country.
I understand that the province of Quebec owns almost 90 percent of forest lands in that province.
The national forest production reached almost $2 billion in 1959. As for exports, they amounted to nearly $1.5 billion.
The prime minister of Russia realizes to what extent the forest industry is important in this country because, not so long ago, he sent a special mission to Canada to study the manufacture of newsprint. He even went further. He warned Canadians and Americans that, in five or six years from now, he would get into the paper market. If lacking in other qualities, Mr. Khrushchev has at least that of being frank in certain respects, and he advises us in advance of the difficulties we will have to face. So that the outlook for our exports of newsprint is rather dark, unless we take the necessary steps to meet the problem which lies in wait for us.
Nobody can deny it. Our forest resources are a most precious asset in the natural wealth of this country, particularly in the province of Quebec. But are we, in Quebec, and in Canada as a whole, aware of the importance of protecting the asset which the natural wealth of our forests represents?
As far as we, in Quebec, are concerned, we made, in 1950 a very adequate study of the question of the natural wealth we have in our forests. In my province, the forest engineers' association has considered the problem. Forest engineers have examined the question with much devotion and efficiency. They submitted to the government of my province a report which has now become famous, in connection with the forest problem in Quebec. One of the best known papers of Quebec-I have named he Soleil-published a detailed summary of the Quebec forest engineers' report, I shall simply quote two or three excerpts of the very concrete and positive recommendations made therein. The report was published in Le Soleil in November 1957.
Each year, in our province, enormous quantities of timber are taken out of the woods, leaving

in the area nothing but stumps, and as seed bearers only defective trees which, in many cases, become centres of infection and of devastating diseases. Without improved cutting and a better cleaning up of lumbering sites, it will be almost impossible to ensure the survival of healthy growth, and to put back into our forest what was taken out by timber cutting.
And further on, Mr. Speaker, the report says:
In order to remedy that urgent situation, the association of forest engineers advocated the creation of a provincial research organization-
And here, Mr. Speaker, I quote the very words of the report of the Quebec forest engineers' association.
-which alone would be in a position to give guidance in sound forestry practices and to establish our forest policy on solid foundations. Among the most urgent forest studies to be undertaken, it was recommended that consideration be given to an inventory of our wooded areas, so as to establish not only the extent, the composition, the volume, the age and the rate of growth of our forests, but also to foresee, in keeping with our economical and social structure, the role they may play as an industrial or agricultural expansion territory, as a reservoir of raw material or as a protective agent for our animals and water resources.
In that same report, the forest engineers' association outlines its fears. It says that if the matter is not considered more closely, there is danger that our forest industry, in 20 to 60 years, may disappear, unless very energetic steps are taken in this field. As for those energetic steps, two recommendations are mentioned, first the reforestation of developed areas and, second, an increased rate of growth of the forest resources remaining in Quebec.
The report also indicates that one of the most rational solutions to be put into practice in our province is:
To rely upon the data provided by scientific research and forest experiments.
And the report goes on to say:
Of all necessity, the industry, in its own interest, will have to do this as soon as possible, first to maintain itself, and to avoid the possible ruin of one of the major sectors of our economy.
The study of the Quebec forest engineers' association goes on to emphasize scientific organization, without which our forest industry could not maintain itself nor face ouside competition.
I very well remember that it is none other than the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself who pointed out that aspect of the matter when talking about this bill in Montreal a few months ago.

Finally, allow me to quote a few excerpts from the conclusions of the brief:
The state is in duty bound to encourage research by means of substantial financial participation-
And, Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize these words:
-by means of substantial financial participation to the work already being carried out in existing institutions, and by the development of higher forestry teaching, whereby the technicians required by industry and the experts who are indispensable to the advancement of science may be trained.
I hope that the officers of those private industries developing our natural forest resources will not be offended if I go as far as to suggest that our forest industries should make their own financial contributions to that research the federal government wants to promote by establishing, at the national level, a department of forestry.
There is nothing surprising in the suggestion if one considers that such a contribution from our industries would be not only for the common good, not only to the benefit of our people, who are in fact the true owners of our natural resources, but also to the benefit of private industry, since it will be able to enjoy much longer the natural resources which it is developing generally in our province and in our country.
As I was saying a moment ago, the province of Quebec owns close to 90 per cent of the natural forestry resources found in the province. The Quebec provincial government has a very heavy responsibility in the conservation and reforestation of that natural resource; it must therefore do its share in co-operation with private industry which, in a sense, holds a lease on this natural wealth, not only for its own benefit but also for the benefit of every Quebec citizen. I know the new Quebec government-and this is in no way intended as petty politics-recognizes the fact that this wealth belongs to the citizens of Quebec. The new government has undertaken to arrange for the citizens of my province to get greater benefits out of this natural wealth, and I hope with all my heart that it will keep its promise.
We have had enough of politicians who travel through Canada's provinces, making promises that they keep in the background once they have got themselves elected. Personally, if the hon. premier of Quebec should some day decide to change his name for that of the Prime Minister of my country, I would not hesitate a single moment to denounce him; however, I know my provincial premier well enough to know he
Forestry Department
would not go that far. It is in his own interest. It is particularly in the interest of the citizens of my province, that he keep his word and honour his solemn pledges to my fellow citizens of Quebec.
That is the reason why most members or candidates who supported Mr. Lesage talked about the natural wealth of my province. They discussed its forestry resources.
There has been much talk about planning. A few years ago, whenever anyone mentioned planning, I was a bit shocked because no one had ever told me what the word meant in the minds of those who used it. However, after giving the matter much thought, I came to the conclusion that the word planning had been quite thoroughly put into practice by the former Liberal administration in Ottawa. The Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent and all the ministers who shared his task of running the country did not just look after present-day needs. They looked to the future of this country. They did not administer in view of 1956 or 1955, but considered the whole twentieth century, and when you look to the future and plan for what is coming, I think that is planning. I also think the government of my province will do some planning in regard to Quebec's natural forestry resources.
The bill placed before us by the federal administration will certainly arouse certain provincial governments. We have had in Quebec-and in this connection I recognize the merits of the former Quebec government -a nucleus of research in the field of forestry. I realize it was not enough, but I must admit the former leaders of Quebec did understand, according to their own lights, the significance of forestry resources for Quebec. They had at least made a start, and for that I must commend them. I hope the new administration will realize to a greater extent what the Quebec forests mean for the people of the province. The Quebec forests, Mr. Speaker, are more or less the backbone of the whole provincial economy. In view of that, I have some misgivings in examining the bill before us, an act respecting the department of forestry.
In fact, referring to subsection 9 on page 3, for instance, there are two paragraphs about which I have certain misgivings as to provincial and federal jurisdictions. Here is what I find:
The governor in council may make regulations for the protection, care and management of forest

Forestry Department
experimental areas, and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations respecting
(a) the cutting, removal and disposal of timber, the establishment and use of reservoirs, waterpower sites, power transmission lines, telegraph and telephone lines, and any other use not inconsistent with the purposes of this act, and the granting of leases and permits therefor;
And subsection (e) reads as follows:
the removal and exclusion of trespassers and of persons failing to comply with the regulations; and
(f) the prevention of trespass, mutilation or destruction of trees and destruction or damaging of buildings, materials or notices used in connection with the administration or management of any forest experimental area.
As regard to property, timber cutting permits, exploitation permits, it seems to me that by this legislation the federal government is interfering with the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures.

speechtext:
I was listening very carefully to the hon. member describing the regulations in clause 9. Would he also read clause 7 to the house which has to do with all the following clauses relating to forest experimental areas?
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I understand perfectly well the very timely question asked by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. But why not simply stick to clause 7? Why was it deemed advisable to add clause 9 in this bill? I hope that the minister will give me the answer to that question when he speaks at the end of the debate on this bill. Because that raises questions in my mind as to the constitutionality of clause 9, even though clause 7 indicates clearly, that:
The governor in council may establish as a forest experimental area lands belonging to Her Majesty in right of Canada and may at any time withdraw lands from or add lands to a forest experimental area.
In my opinion, the federal government assumes the right by section 7, to decide that such or such part of that province will come under its own jurisdiction. That is what I am wondering about. Then, if the hon. minister would give us his interpretation of

those two sections, this will be quite useful to me for, if he gives me a satisfying interpretation, I will be satisfied. If, on the other hand, I do not understand it, I will ask further explanations to friends who are more competent than I, but I will be quite glad to accept the explanations that will be given to me.
In the meantime, I wonder if those two sections, and section 9 in particular, are not in flagrant conflict with subsection 5 of subsection 92 of the British North America Act.
So, I will wait quite patiently for the information that the hon. minister who sponsored this bill will give us.
This subsection 5 of section 92 of the British North America Act indicates that the exclusive right to make laws on the management and sale of public lands belonging to the provinces, as well as the forests thereon, is strictly of provincial jurisdiction.
Again, I want to be fair to the minister and I am quite willing to subordinate section 9 to section 7, to which he just referred. But I am anxious to hear his comments on this matter. All I can hope for in the meantime, is that not only the jurisdiction of the provinces will be respected in the wording of the bill, but that the authority of the ten provinces of my country will be respected in fact as well as in practice.
Besides, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources understands the situation, since he took part in a discussion in the province of Quebec-it was in February last, I believe-at the convention of the Canadian Lumbermen's Association, a discussion in which representatives of Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia also participated. And the fear I am expressing today has been expressed by the late Jacques Miquelon-when I say the "late", I mean politically, of course, because he is not dead-and I would like to quote on this matter an article from the Gazette of February 17, 1960, entitled:
(Text):
$10 Million for Federal Forest Research
The new federal department of forestry will spend $10 million a year on basic research, Hon. Alvin Hamilton, federal Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, revealed here yesterday.
Mr. Hamilton made the statement in a panel discussion with forestry ministers from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario at the second day of the convention of the Canadian lumbermen's association.

He declared that the present federal forestry research staff would be nearly doubled within the next five years but would not duplicate the present work of provincial forestry research.
(Translation):
At this point, I would like to point out to the house that I hope the new department of forestry of the federal government will have not only a negative effect, in the sense it will avoid a duplication of research in the provinces, but also a positive effect, that of bringing co-ordination in the field of forestry research in Canada.
(Text):
The federal minister made this statement after Hon. Jacques Miquelon, Q.C., Quebec minister of lands and forests, declared: "We have good reasons to fear this federal initiative and would have to oppose it if it constitutes an encroachment on the undisputable and exclusive rights of the province of Quebec on forestry matters."
(Translation):
I should like to go further than the hon. Jacques Miquelon and not mention only the province of Quebec because, after all, the province of Quebec is not the only province in this country. There are ten provinces in Canada and I hope that the new department will not infringe upon any legislative jurisdiction of the provinces of my country.
In other words I hope the new department will not interfere in any field within the jurisdiction of any province of my country, neither in Quebec nor in the nine other provinces, I hope that the time is past when it was thought that Quebec was the only province in Canada. Quebec is one of the ten provinces of Canada and I hope it will no longer be said that Quebec is the only province forming part of the Canadian confederation.
I am not the only one to express fear as to the federal jurisdiction in the field of forestry.
One has only to read the papers to note this fact, Le Soleil for instance, which for some time can no longer be considered a Liberal paper, reported on January 23, 1960, the reactions of various papers across the country respecting the establishment of a federal department of forestry.
I should like to quote part of this item entitled:
The new federal department
The establishment of a new department to deal with forestry matters which was announced in the speech from the throne, naturally causes particular concern in Ontario and Quebec.
Le Droit had this to say:
Everybody knows that forest development is one of the main industries of those two provinces-
Forestry Department
Will the federal government attempt to interfere in provincial matters It is stated that the new department will concern itself mostly with research: production methods, sales methods, etc. It will co-ordinate the various existing forestry services, will improve them in order to be of greater help to the provinces and industries in increasing production, in finding outlets on foreign markets, etc.
Such must be, in fact, the new department: an organization to give help and co-operation, nothing more. But will it limit itself to that? This is the important question.
Between "co-operation" and "intervention", between "assistance" and "pressure", the margin might be very slim indeed, at times. What is, in the opinion of federal authorities, a simple measure of assistance, might well be infringement in the eye of provincial authorities.
And when I speak about provincial authorities, I wish to point out again that it is not only the province of Quebec which is concerned. The province of Quebec is only one of the ten provinces of my country. And when I speak of interference in provincial legislatures, I mean all ten legislatures in Canada.
If the department which the federal government intends to establish merely co-ordinates research, merely advises and helps the provinces in the field of research, not only do I see no objection, but I welcome the establishment of a department of forestry in Canada.
I think it is in the general interest. I also think that the establishment of such a department will help arouse some provinces which are inactive in that field.
Under those conditions, I shall wholeheartedly support the establishment of such a department. But, on the other hand, I shall be one of its most eager antagonists if, after it is established, there is any attempt of any kind to interfere with the issue of permits which the provinces alone have the right to give.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I shall become an eager opponent of that department and I hope also that my colleagues from Quebec and from the other provinces, concerned about the rights of the provinces, will not hesitate to support me.
So long as the federal department of forestry is interested only in research, and is content to promote research, so long as it is interested only in providing advice to the provincial legislatures with a view to protecting one of the greatest natural wealth of our country and of my province in particular, then I commend most sincerely the establishment of this new department and I am anxious to see it in operation, to see it achieve useful and even necessary things and obtain concrete results in our country.

Forestry Department
I also hope that the provinces, realizing that the forests which cover 40 per cent of our territory, represent one of the greatest assets in Canada, will understand that we must not only do everything in their power to reforest, but also to obtain that individuals and corporations which have timber permits will themselves contribute to the reforestation.
If the provincial and federal legislatures as well as the private industries of Canada realize the importance of doing that, I am sure that all of us will have been very useful to our country, to Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I represent people who for the greater part depend for their living on the lumber industry, I would be remiss if I did not rake this opportunity of saying a few words on the legislation now before us and of pointing out, as did other hon. members before me, the importance of that industry, not only for my riding, but for the country as a whole.
Hon. members who preceded me quoted some figures which are, as a matter of fact, most eloquent, and show the vital importance of our forests.
Let us, indeed, consider that our lumber industry comes first in this country in terms of employment, salaries, new investments, and net production value.
In terms of gross national product, it is superior to, and even twice as important, as the production of our operating mines. In the last ten years, forests have produced between 29 and 36 per cent of Canada's exports.
Their importance is all the more evident when we consider that they are a net asset for the country, that is to say that the value of exports exceeds by far the value of imports.
In 1958, for instance, their net assets reached $1,180 million (U.S.).
We may say, therefore, that this industry is probably, if not certainly, our most important source of American currency.
In 1959, 115,000 persons were employed directly in forest operations; and if we consider all the secondary industries deriving from our forests, we realize as the minister indicated, that they represent the most important and substantial sector of our economic life.
In 1959, their total production reached $2,100 million of which $1,400 million worth were exported.
[Mr. Brassard (Lapointe).3
In 1959, total production of dressed lumber amounted to 7.3 billion feet. Dressed lumber exports amounted to $323 million an increase of 10.5 per cent over 1958 which is 57 per cent of the total production. These figures are a very tangible proof of the importance of that industry. The seriousness with which this matter was discussed in the house today and the attention of all the members go to show the importance of the lumber industry.
And what is actually the outlook for that industry? The minister dealt with the subject when he said that the demand for paper products not only in Canada but in the whole world amounted to 56 metric tons in 1955 and that it was expected that that total would reach 86 metric tons in 1965 and 134 metric tons in 1975.
Today, Canada accounts for 16 per cent of the international consumption of paper and paper products. According to the most accurate estimations, an increase of 123 per cent will be apparent in the universal consumption of these products between 1955 and 1975. Canada will therefore have to increase its production accordingly if it wants to retain the same percentage of the world market. Despite the growing needs in the world, due to the industrial development that took place in many countries, our position does certainly not leave the government and the authorities unconcerned. One of the reasons for this concern is the increasingly important part played in this field of world trade by the Soviet union. This part affects our country directly.
Since 1954, despite a growing demand for wood products and by-products, our wood and forest products exports to Great Britain fell by almost 50 per cent. However, there was an increase of 75 per cent in imports from the Soviet union.
Those are upsetting statistics, if we realize that there is growing demand for this kind of product. It is true that Russia has succeeded in increasing its export by commercial practices that might be called disloyal. For instance, that country resorted to what we call the "fall clause", which consists in lowering the price of a product to the lowest level at which another country may supply it.
All of which clearly shows that the government should seriously consider enabling our industry to compete on even terms with the others, and this is precisely the object of

this bill. It aims at promoting research with regard to the protection, management and use of our forest resources. This legislation tends to ensure a wiser use of forest products by establishing research laboratories for instance. Another aspect consists in setting up new techniques in the captivating field of wood chemistry, by which the most extraordinary products like explosives and similar items may be obtained.
The people may also be encouraged to co-operate in the protection and rational use of our forest resources by propagating, for instance, in a scientific manner, the means of preserving our timber resources against the plague of fire, by disseminating information and increasing general awareness among the public with regard to forest conservation.
There is another field which the new department will be called upon to control. I am speaking of the administration of forest domains in the territories which are the responsibility of the federal government.
The new n.inister might also conclude some agreements in respect of research with all provinces that are willing to do so.
And, finally it is intended to merge the forest biology division which is now under the Department of Agriculture with a staff of 405 and the forestry branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. This latter division has at this time a staff of 426.
Another part, quite important this one, that this department will be able to play will be to supply the smaller forestry enterprises with very accurate data on research in the field of new forestry techniques.
Such Mr. Speaker, is the wide field of action of this new department. It is true that it will absorb certain existing divisions, but others will certainly be created. However what is surely the most important point is that there will be from now on only one agency to manage this immeasurable wealth of our forests.
Contrary to the suggestion made on the other side of the house, I think the appointment of a new minister to run this department is a necessity. If the department is to really carry out its duties, as indicated by the hon. minister who sponsored the bill, it will have to look after many administrative details.
Some members have expressed the fear that the new department will be a threat to provincial rights. Mention has been made of provincial autonomy in the forestry field, 79951-0-383
Forestry Department
and rightly so, because under the constitution, forests located on public lands or crown lands come directly under the provinces. However, there is no intention, in setting up this new department, to encroach on provincial rights. The provinces are being offered-and they are absolutely free to accept or refuse-research services which such a federal department will certainly be in a better position to provide efficiently than ten separate provincial departments. Special arrangements may also be made with the provinces if they wish. And to confirm that, this bill only deals with matters coming under federal jurisdiction, one has only to refer to section 5 of the bill, which reads as follows:
The duties, powers and functions of the minister extend to and include all matters over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction relating to the forest resources of Canada.
The important words in this section are therefore the following:
... all matters over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction relating to the forest resources of Canada.
The bill is therefore quite clear on that point. It only deals with matters coming under the Canadian parliament. There is no invasion, no encroachment on provincial rights in this field. Section 5, which is a general section, serves as an interpretative clause for some of the other sections which deal with details, such as section 6.
The hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) wondered whether section 9, and particularly subsections (a) and (e) which refer to regulations on woodcutting and other such subjects, might involve an invasion of provincial rights. Well, this section is under part II of the bill, which bears the following heading:
Forest experimental areas.
That part II begins with section 7 which says:
The governor in council may establish as a forest expermiental area lands belonging to Her Majesty in right of Canada-
Therefore, it is laid down there, in so many words, that it is really lands belonging to Her Majesty in right of Canada. Furthermore, the regulations outlined in section 9 obviously concern lands belonging to Her Majesty, where forest experimental areas will have been or will be established.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the bill cannot be clearer on that point. Besides the explanatory note on that part reads as follows:
Part II provides for the establishment of forest experimental areas on lands belonging to Her Majesty in right of Canada and for the making of regulations affecting such areas.

Forestry Department
Therefore, in the bill as it is now worded there is definitely no sign whatever of anything that might lead one to suspect that the government wishes to intervene in a field which, by its very expression, and by the very declaration of the government and of its ministers, belongs entirely to the provinces. It is merely a question of helping those who are in need, in providing them with services which, we submit, only the federal government is in a position to provide in a fully adequate way.
Mr. Speaker, our forest operation methods have changed substantially over the last few years. Forest industry, as many others, is now in the era of automation, of mechanization and of specialized tools. It was the old-fashioned lumberjacks who opened up this country, and when I say this country, I mean my own part of the country. It is very dear to my heart indeed this Ottawa valley district, whose development is certainly due, in great part, to those pioneers who went up the majestic waters of the Ottawa and its tributaries, the Gatineau, the Coulonge, the Lievre, the Du Moine. Pages full of heroic episodes have been written about those people who certainly knew what hard work meant. They also knew very deep joys and sorrows.
Today, they are not called woodsmen or lumberjacks any more but forest workers. They are equipped with mechanical chains, mechanical saws and preceded by heavy machinery, bulldozers which clear the way for them. They live in conditions of luxury which our forerunners, the pioneers of this valley certainly never imagined. All that is progress, and it is the hallmark of our time. But, when leaving an era which is now gone forever, we cannot but think with some nostalgic feeling of all the great deeds which have been recorded and which are an essential part of our folklore.
Mr. Speaker, as I said at the start, our forest industry, with all its by-products, has become the most significant in our country. Throughout the world it occupies a more and more important place. That is why the government is creating a new department, which is a tangible proof of its wish to safeguard that prime wealth of our country not only for the remote future, but even for the generations yet unborn.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the result of all this research, these studies of development techniques, will be that the forests, the whole field of the lumber industry will be considered somehow like tilled ground carrying renewable crops, and we will thus

have a permanent wealth in timber, and an everlasting productivity.
With all the care the government is bringing and that the average citizen should bring to the question, we will preserve for a long time splendid resources which the forest industry is able to offer, and that green curtain which is our very symbol and which every right-thinking Canadian should love. The forest, as I say, is not only a source of wealth, it is a place for recreation.
I believe that it is a very important part of the forest and that it should be kept up by setting up, together with the provinces, rules and regulations for its conservation and preservation against fire.
We will reach that double aim if we endeavour on the one hand to conserve our resources, and on the other hand, to offer all Canadians unequalled opportunities for recreation.
