During the resolution stage I expressed our approval of the bill and what it set out to do. I sometimes think we are so partisan in the house that we forget to compliment people who have been instrumental in introducing legislation that we do like, and for that reason I wish to say to the minister that I appreciate the fact that he and at least one or two other members of the cabinet were able to crystallize the recommendations of the House of Commons committee into something which was even a little more than some of us had expected we would get.
It has often been a rather fond House of Commons view that committee work in the House of Commons turns out to be inconsequential because recommendations are not given much effect. It seems to me that in this case we can thank the minister and others for making a move in a direction of which the committee approves and, generally, carrying out the sense of the committee's wishes.
The department may, of course, be weak or strong. Much depends on the personalities concerned and on what the government is prepared to do. I would suggest to the minister that forestry is a most important aspect of the Canadian economy. I remember that when I said that before in the house several years ago there were some objections but I think the ramifications of the industry and what it means in terms of employment are better known now than they were two years ago.

The new department will remove from the present minister some of his many duties, and in that sense it may not only lead to the betterment of forestry but it may do something for northern affairs and national resources. Incidentally, I am interested in whether we are to see a shortening of the minister's present title. It is a small point, but it seems to me that the hon. gentleman or anyone in charge of that department might become better known if the name were shortened. I know that "northern affairs" is not an apt description of the work of the department as long as it is responsible for museums, national parks and certain other branches which now come under its jurisdiction. However, I certainly feel that the present title is too long. When the new department is set up, I hope it will not have a cumbersome title, such as the department of forestry and regeneration services, or department of forestry and forest products research, or anything such as that.
The bill is a simple one and there is nothing extraordinary in what it sets out as far as the scope of the new department is concerned. In fact, it is really only a bringing together of the forestry activities of the government under one heading. The essence, I suppose, is the opportunity for united leadership and we are looking forward to that.
One of the points I want to talk about is this. When you look at this department you see that it is going to have two natural divisions: one on the forestry side and the other on the forest products side. I wanted to concentrate upon the forestry aspect, the whole business of silviculture, regeneration, forest access roads and especially the role of the professional forester in this matter.
In Canada today we have only four professional foresters for every 4,000 square miles of merchantable timber which is not very many. I cannot think of any professional group which has less influence in relation to the economic milieu in which they work, namely that of forestry. They have been very slow at reaching the top of the business side of their work, and there tends to be quite a split between the government foresters and the industrial foresters.
Hon. members may wonder why I would go as far as to make that statement. I live in an area and have worked at a job that brought me in touch with foresters, and we have a very large number of them relatively in our area although, compared with an area of some 140,000 square miles the figure is not so large.
There is quite a suspicion amongst foresters, especially the industrial foresters who tend 79951-0-383J
Forestry Department
to look upon the government forester as an idealistic chap who has not much sense of economics. He tends to feel that since he is the man who marks out the wood and gets it to the mill he is doing a very important job. On the other hand, the government foresters, who are almost equal in number to the industrial foresters in Canada, have a suspicion of the industrial foresters and feel that the attitudes of the companies that cut our wood are linked up more with the quarterly dividends and the annual reports than they are with the long term view that is needed in forestry matters.
This rivalry is always evident at most get-togethers where the professional foresters consort to talk about their problems. I have been to a number of their meetings which have usually wound up in a bit of a blow-up and hard feelings, and so on all around. Most of this took place between provincial and industrial foresters, since that is where the nexus is so hard, because along with every province in Canada the provincial foresters are the ones who regulate and carry out the statutes of the provinces, in so far as cutting, scaling, regeneration practices and the direct forestry approach are concerned, and naturally as the supervisors with punitive powers the industrial foresters tend to look askance at them. Many times the federal department of forestry has never had the stature, in my view, to act in the role that I think it might do and take some of the heat off provincial foresters and industrial foresters themselves and act more as co-ordinating foresters in getting an over-all pattern, an advisory pattern, in developing really good forestry management policies.
A good friend of mine, a professional forester, last year gave a speech that I think made this point quite well, and I want to read an excerpt from it. It appeared in the Globe and Mail of January 17, and was delivered in Sudbury. It reads in part as follows:
A four-point program to cover the lack of an official Canadian forest management policy to insure perpetuation of the country's forests and maintenance of its competitive position in world forest products was outlined here today by K. W. Hearnden, Abitibi Power and Paper Company Limited divisional forester at Port Arthur.
Addressing the annual meeting of the Ontario professional foresters association, he said the program should include: establishment of silvicultural standards by the profession; a professional campaign for forest management legislation; public education in forestry and the profession's problems, and professional authority to create and maintain forest management policies.
"This deficiency is apparent in the legislation of most provinces where regulations are made to insure the orderly liquidation of virgin stands, and to provide for the levying of stumpage assessments, taxes, rentals and penalties," he said.

Forestry Department
The forester in industry derives little or no support from either the public's general attitude to the forests or from existing legislation, Mr. Hearn-den contended.
The industrial forester is not only unable to practice his profession, but does not feel free to express his views on it and seldom does, the speaker said.
"This is equally true of foresters in government employ" Mr. Hearnden said. "This accounts for the efforts of most foresters, particularly in junior positions, to avoid the limelight... he steers clear of the unpopular and resigns himself to the support of policies of expediencies."
Mr. Hearnden listed several other factors as "deterrents to forest management and the discharge of professional duties in industry."
These included steadily mounting labour costs in timber production; lack of a long term objective in forest management; lack of authority by most professional foresters in industry to manage the forest "in any real sense;" a strong, psychological influence against the practice of forestry in Ontario; slow development of access roads into forest areas, and a shortage of professional foresters and forest technicians in Canada.
This is not a particularly attractive picture that has been painted by one of the keenest professional foresters, and yet I think it is a good summary of the situation. The professional forester tends to feel that he has an analysis of the forest that can bring the best to the country not only in economic returns but also in social returns in the use of the forest for camping, fishing and wildlife and those sorts of matters; but he really has not today either the reputation or the feeling of a very wide kind. I have always felt that one of the main reasons for this has been the very close connection between the awarding of timber limits and the opportunity to make money. When you have that cash consideration or the opportunity of making money tied in with the resources of the crown that are disposed of in the hands of politicians, provincial politicians-I do not say "politicians" in any bad way-it is very hard to get an over-all management problem approach that is very sound. The foresters in the main tended to bog down in the middle echelon of industrial organization.
I know of very few who have attained great stature. I suppose Mr. MacMillan of MacMillan and Bloedel Limited is the most outstanding example. He was one of the first foresters in the federal service. I remember reading a report in 1908 on forest surveys, a statistical report on the depletion of the white pine, and that was created by Mr. MacMillan, but he is almost an isolated example of a forester rising to a high and effective managerial post in industry. They tend to bog down lower down.
The professional education of foresters is concentrated in the four universities in Canada, and from my knowledge of the position of the faculties in forestry on the various

campuses, they are not considered to be extremely important segments, perhaps with the exception of New Brunswick where the forestry faculty has more stature perhaps than does the faculty in Toronto. The foresters have to contend with, work for or work with one of the 11 government agencies that exist in Canada, and this bill points out the difficulty in that. If you have 11 different standards of forest management and 11 different ways of getting money for the crown from the forest plan, you have a very wide differentiation, as we have in Canada, between the kind of foresters we have. It is little wonder that it has been very hard to get an over-all forestry policy.
A further difficulty of the forester has been that there has been a tremendous increase in specialization in the industry. Some of the men who have gone ahead the fastest have not been those who have anything to do with silvicultural programs but those in the field of photogrammetry or forest economics or who go into the logging side of the picture. As a consequence, year by year even within the foresters that we do have there is an erosion in the role they can play as foresters, and it seems to me this thinning out has done a lot of harm to the profession in terms of the impact it makes.
There has been a tremendous change too in the way we use wood. There is a contention among some people in the forest industry that it really does not matter what kind of species you grow or where you grow them as long as you get a cellulose return on acres somewhere after you have a cut-over. There is another argument so far as our forests are concerned which was very well put by a University of Toronto professor of economics who tended to argue that those who worry too much about the future conservation of the forests are missing the tremendous changes that are taking place in our techniques. He has argued that too much concern for 50, 60 or 70 years from now with relation to our forests may be completely useless because by that time technical improvisation will have ended the need for the forests as we look at them today.
These are all factors that tend to disturb and undermine the position of the professional forester and his belief, which is usually very strongly held, that by proper forest management you can have the right tree on the right site in the right place for its economic use and that you can have things on a sustained yield basis. One of the truisms or cliches that has come to be accepted in forestry in Canada has to do with the matter of sustained yield. Almost any provincial minister of forestry or minister in charge of

lands and forests will sound off at least once a year to the effect that the provincial forests are on a sustained yield basis, but the question always seems to remain, sustained yield in relation to what?
One thing that we in the Port Arthur region know is that we still have a tremendous amount of both conifers and hardwoods but we are not using hardwoods nearly as much as conifers. Each year means going a little bit farther from the mills for the wood and because of the large scale capital expenditure in the mills the result is that wood is getting more and more expensive and the sites closer to the mills are becoming more and more attractive. Yet it is pretty hard to argue that some of our cut-overs that are within easy trucking distance of the mills are on any kind of sustained yield basis or that regeneration standards are high enough.
It is a very moot question whether there should be more planning done and whether scarification should be required on all cutover sites. There is even an argument that the pulp and paper industry should get away more from clear cutting and get into sheltered cutting or strip cutting or various devices like that which will allow some kind of seeding-in process and at the same time will not lead to too many blow-downs or the death of trees by sun scalding.
All these factors make it very hard to appreciate the true sustained yield picture. It is very easy to take Ontario and get some idea after a large scale survey as to merchantable timber and to figure out rough increments by year for the various species and to say, "Well, we are cutting so many cords and so many cords are growing so we are away." But I insist that you should consider sustained yield in relation to the unit that is using the particular area of the forest, and from that point of view there are very many parts of Canada in which the forests are being exploited and are not on a sustained yield basis.
One of the commentaries on this is the fact that we have not been able to get capital to go in and establish pulp mills in many places where we have virgin forests. I can think of northern Saskatchewan and northern Manitoba. Western Ontario also has sufficient forest land to support at least one or perhaps two more mills. I have noted that Crown Zellerbach decided not to go ahead in Newfoundland not too long ago despite the fact that there are adequate supplies there of standing and potential timber. This indicates to me that our idea of Canadian forests being on a sound sustained yield management basis is rather incorrect and is all the more reason
Forestry Department
why we should have a vigorous co-ordination of management projection and the ideal kind of forest management on the part of the federal forestry department.
The fact that we are getting into a tougher and tougher competitive situation at least in the short run so far as our forest products are concerned is also very serious. I think that here again the situation is tougher in the short run and will be harder in the long run.
On the lumber side of things, especially in eastern Canada, it seems to me that the new department has to do even more than the forest products section has done in implementing standards. On the lumbering side I think one of the things we are going to have to have in eastern Canada is the kind of marketing set-up that the western lumber producers have been able to organize such as Seaboard Lumber Sales. There are so many producers of lumber in the eastern woods who have not got a common set of standards. I am not denegating the attempts they are making to get these standards but they still have not got them.
Much Canadian lumber has very great difficulty moving in export markets just because there are very great doubts, particularly in the European market, about the standards of some of our lumber, especially in the spruce field. I understand this does not apply to the products turned out in British Columbia but it certainly does to those of eastern Canada.
It seems to me there will have to be a great deal of effort by the new department to get better operating methods in the woods for small lumber producers and a common marketing agency that will set standards and will also have available export credits and the ability to sell lumber. The Department of Trade and Commerce through its trade commissioner service does this now to a degree but I would imagine they would welcome efforts toward a co-ordination on the part of the eastern Canadian lumber industry and the new department in order to place more of our eastern Canadian lumber in the European market and also the United States market.
It seems to me that in the short run the prospect for the pulp and paper industry is not as bad as on the lumber side. In the long run I think its prospects are excellent just in terms of the growth of the use of newsprint and of various papers for packaging. But there is no question at the present time that Canada in the main has about the highest pulp cost of any part of the world that is in direct competition. I understand that people in the pulp and paper industry say that at the present time the Swedes can

Mr. Speaker, this particular bill setting up the department of forestry is of major importance to Canada as a whole and of paramount importance to British Columbia. The minister, in introducing the bill this afternoon, gave a few figures and stated that in 1957 the value of forest products was $2.2 billion; the value of exports that year of forest products was $1.4 billion or 65 per cent of the total production. In British Columbia I believe we export about 80 per cent of our production. The economy of British Columbia is directly geared to the prosperity of our forest industries, so thal as they go so goes the rest of the province. Ir this regard the long range forecast, of course, is good.
As has been pointed out, the anticipated growth by 1980 is at least 50 per cent in sawn timber and 90 per cent in pulp and paper, according to the figures given by the minister, and one source has the consumption of pulp and paper up to 140 per cent increase by 1975. The problem of course we are faced with is not only the utilization of our resources but the utilization of those resources at costs which will allow us to compete in the world market. In that regard I should like to quote from the 1958 standing committee on mines, forests and waters. Mr. Ian S. Mahood, an outstanding forester from British Columbia, in testimony at that time stated as follows as found at page 355 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of that committee:
It should be clearly appreciated that B.C. faces a unique and unusual circumstance in its position with respect to export markets. In almost all our traditional market areas, with particular emphasis on the United States southern pine region,- Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Britain, a high standard of forest cultivation is being achieved. There are dynamc increases in the domestic supplies in these regions. In some cases the trees being grown are B.C. Douglas fir, spruce and hemlock, transplanted, harvested and converted into commercial products at lower cost than we in B.C. can harvest, process and deliver the like to distant markets.
Much has been said of the large forest areas that we have. I believe it was mentioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) that our forest areas represent 40 per cent of the land area of the provinces as compared with 10 per cent devoted to agriculture. However, these areas are not all economical to work at the present time. They may be of value at some time in the future but at the present time the cost of transportation of forest products to the processing

Forestry Department
plants and to the mills is of paramount importance and it is necessary to have a strong program of regeneration, of forest planting, of forest management, of tree farming, as the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) said, in order to have a sustained yield-again in this matter I differ with my friend the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher)-in those areas which are close enough to the mills to be economic.
In tree farming there is a great deal that we must do and that we must learn. It is in this area that I believe this new department will have its greatest effect. As the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 5486 of Hansard:
The conduct of forest and forest products research has been for many years a function of the dominion government, which now has unusually well developed research facilities in this field, toy a wide margin the strongest of those facilities.
That is in comparison with the provinces. It is in that area this department can have the greatest effect. Mr. Mahood in his testimony pointed out that 30 years ago in the southern pine region of the United States forest production was grinding to a halt, but that by careful treatment, by the scientific application of good forestry methods to this area, it has now become one of the major forest products areas of the United States.
If in the field of agriculture, we had stayed with Indian maize and had not had any hybridization or development of hard wheat or wheat which would mature quickly in the far north, wheat which would withstand drought, we would not have much of a wheat crop. The same thing has been done with regard to food animals, fruits, vegetables and flowers. But today all we do is that we use the same tree which has been the same for thousands of years, we replant that tree or let it naturally repeat itself and that tree is the crop for tomorrow. We do this instead of looking out and trying to develop hybrid trees which would perhaps have fire resistant bark, trees which will mature much more quickly than our natural growth trees, trees which will have the proper chemical composition, the proper characteristics for the purposes for which they are to be used. It is in this area that this department can be of inestimable value to economy of my province.
I do not want to take much of the time of the committee but for the sake of the record I suggest that the question of access roads, the question of training fire fighters, the question perhaps of the use of airplanes in fighting fires can be given consideration. I know that planes are now being used in British Columbia in order to scoop up water 
and take it to the site of fires. It is not perfectly successful as yet but the development of the use of planes in fire fighting may be in the way of making a water fog, as was suggested by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. McQuillan) who is certainly an expert on forestry methods and knows as much about forestry as does anybody in this house. There is a great deal of room for the work of this department in order to make a major contribution to the economy of this country and a contribution to the industry which has perhaps the greatest growth factor of any of our industries.
I am indeed pleased that this government has gone ahead with this proposal. In conclusion I should like to say this. It also seems to me to be a justification, if that is needed, or perhaps an example of the wisdom of our Prime Minister when he got so many committees working and when he threw so many problems to the committee to thresh out. As you know, Mr. Speaker, this is a direct result of the recommendations made by the standing committee on mines, forests and waters. It is an indication of what can be done. It is an indication of what can be done with a good committee when it is given the time in which to study a job and the authority to go into it in detail.

If I rise to speak on second reading of this Bill No. C-82, to establish the new ministry of forestry it is not that I consider myself to be a specialist in the matter but rather that I realize the importance of the studies we are now making and of the functions of the new ministry, inasmuch as it concerns one of the greatest assets of Canada and possibly also because in my riding, namely the riding of Nickel Belt, the forestry industry is one of the major ones. We in the Nickel Belt area have often talked about secondary industries and wished for them. I may say that we should consider forestry as a major industry secondary to mining.
The major companies operating in northern Ontario take much of their raw materials from the area which I represent, namely the K.V.P. Company and the Abitibi Pulp and Paper Company. Also there are major producers operating in my area such as the Plaunt family, the Merwin family and the Poupore family. This industry employs thousands of people yearly. Unfortunately, this year as last year, a reduction has been felt in the operations of the forest industry in northern Ontario. It is for these people that I have a thought when we are discussing the establishment of a new ministry which undoubtedly can bring about a change and

possibly they recognize that at this time the formation of a centralizing body covering the status and possibly the promotion of the industry in Canada will be certainly worthwhile. Many efforts have been made in the past, and we see them in various departments. It has been mentioned in this house that the Department of Trade and Commerce has a branch pertaining to wood products and the northern affairs department also has various research laboratories. There are other departments which carry out functions which in the past have been beneficial to some degree as far as the forestry industry of Canada is concerned.
There are problems in Canada, and the speakers who have preceded me have indicated that studies have been made, but certainly much is to be done. I was reading some of the reports brought to the committee to which I belong, and in one of them it stated that contrary to other branches of our assets in Canada, forestry has not been studied in our universities to the same extent as other subjects. If I recall the exact figures there were only three faculties in Canada which came close to 50 years of existence, and that indicates that for one reason or another the Canadian public has not paid all the attention possible to this subject.
As I read those reports I wondered why it was that Canadians as a whole did not take an interest in this great asset of ours, because the forests of Canada are of great value. However, I read a speech presented by one of the great foresters of Canada, Mr. R. H. MacMillan, when he delivered an address on the fiftieth anniversary of the faculty of forestry at the University of Toronto, and I found the reason why during the last 50 years Canadians have been slow in realizing the efforts which have been made to retain this industry. I should like to quote a paragraph from this speech, and I think hon. members will realize one of the major reasons why the Canadian people as a whole have not paid all the attention possible. Mr. MacMillan said:
Canadians suffer from fixations about their forests. In pioneer days the forest was an obstacle to settlement, to be destroyed at great cost and even hardship; this background may yet be influencing the public attitude against sufficient investment in future forests. The forest is still believed to be inexhaustible and self-perpetuating; it is expected to continue automatically to perform its role as inevitably, cheaply and dependably as the tides. Canadians do not yet fully recognize that the forest, as a crop, is continuously most productive only if there is investment in silvicultural management suited to species and site.
From the numerous literature we have received and the studies we have made all
Forestry Department
hon. members will realize that this trend is disappearing and that industry, as well as government agencies and the public, are much more interested in this last decade or so in this problem than they were previously. In an address which he made I believe last October, Mr. McKee of British Columbia had this to say which I think will be inspiring to the government as well as to the industry of forestry. He said:
To the old-timers in the service it has been a long, uphill fight. To quote our revered old friend, Charlie Holmes, "We have seen public attitude change from hostility to tolerance to co-operation in one short generation." Thus, you will understand why forest service members are pleased to take part in anything which indicates public interest in one of their toughest problems.
If the Canadian public is prepared to accept advance work in this field it is certain that the department which we are just about to create will greatly assist these endeavours.
To indicate to the house the significance of this type of work, as I perceive it not being a specialist, I read a report furnished to me by the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association dated October 1959. In this report I read these striking statistics relating to the use of our forest assets in Canada. The statistics pertain to logs and bolts which take up 42.4 per cent of our forest production per year. By the way, these statistics are based on a 10-year average. Pulp and paper, which is the more prevalent industry in my area, takes up 31.3 per cent. Then I was surprised to learn that fire accounts for 7.5 per cent of our yearly crop yield as our forests are being depleted. I think in this field the new department will be called upon to promote studies and accumulate data relating to our forests.
In this report appears this paragraph which I would like to quote to the house because it indicates that close to 20 per cent of our forest consumption per year is due to destruction by insects and others:
Actually, the percentage of wood consumed by industry is considerably smaller than the foregoing figures indicate for there is also a tremendous annual consumption of wood by diseases, insects, and natural mortality. Although no estimates are yet available, these losses are, at a very maximum, two or three times as great as the average annual loss by fire.
The figure I quoted for fire was 7.5 per cent, so we all realize the loss the Canadian forests sustain from natural causes or diseases. I hope this department will make a great study of the problem and possibly bring about the required changes to save at least half of the loss indicated by this report.
It has been said by previous speakers that Canada has a great role to play in exports of wood products. I have heard that said many

Forestry Department
times, but I was surprised to read in Mr. MacMillan's address that the Marquis of Lansdowne, a former governor general of Canada, as far back as 1885 had some remarks to make on that score on the occasion I believe of the opening of the trans-Canada railway. These words are quoted by Mr. MacMillan in his work, "Fifty years' history of forestry in Canada" and the passage is as follows:
-"very considerable and alarming shrinkage in the timber supply of the world" and went on to say that "the timber-supplying countries of the old world are quite unable to meet the demand made upon them. The forest regions of the great republic which adjoins us have ... been depleted to such an extent that the visible supply will not last for more than a very limited number of years."
As I say, those remarks were made in 1885 and surely if it was visibly true then it is Visibly more true today.
Because of the importance of this industry in Canada, which I consider in northern Ontario is definitely a very important secondary industry to mining, I am very pleased to acknowledge tonight the fact that the department will be formed and that I am prepared to support the bill. I am certain that the department will bring about co-ordination of the work of forestry which is necessary in Canada, which work has been going on to some degree in the last 15 years or so, and this co-ordination will bring about great benefits to the industry of forestry and to Canadians and workers in the industry as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to reaffirm the position which I took in the work of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters with respect to the creation of the department of forestry. I felt at that time, and I am still of the same opinion, that such a department is greatly needed in this dominion of ours, and as one coming from Alberta and from a constituency which has a tremendous forest area -the eastern slope of the Rockies-I feel I should say something in connection with this matter. I hope that those placed in charge of administering this act and promulgating the regulations in part II under clause 9 will take into consideration the multiple uses of an area such as the eastern slope of the Rockies. In other words, we look for an area such as this to provide for our recreation, to provide for the enjoyment of fishing, hunting, wildlife and, above all, to provide grazing lands for the cattlemen who have ranches in the foothills. This latter is a very important part of the proper utilization of the open areas in the forest reserve.
Each summer many cattle are grazed in these areas and I hope that whoever prepares
IMr. Godin.]
the regulations will take into consideration the grazing of livestock and the proper care and use of the range resources. We all know, as has been said by many others, that given care and management, selective cutting and wise economic planning and use of the forest resource should be in the interests of all concerned. It should be a profitable undertaking. In fact, it is so now, but it could be expanded under proper management and as a result of the work which I hope will be encouraged by this new department.
I wish to congratulate the government for having taken up the suggestion of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters and for bringing forward this bill. I want to congratulate the government, the minister and all those who have been concerned with it. I think it is a step forward and I hope it will be put into operation at the earliest possible moment so that we may have in the west and in all parts of Canada some long needed care and management of our forest resources.

I should like to ask the minister to convey to the real sponsor of this bill, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), a suggestion, and the suggestion is this: If the government should decide to accept the advice of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Matthews) rather than the advice of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), with whom, of course, I agree, and if the government should decide to have a separate minister in charge of this department, then I hope the Prime Minister will give consideration to the fact that for three years the province of Newfoundland has been slighted by having a Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Browne). The Minister without Portfolio is a well-known engineer and a man well qualified to preside over this department. In those circumstances Newfoundland will no longer be overlooked unless, of course, this department is being created to provide a portfolio as a peace offering to the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne).

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased tonight to be able to say at the end of the debate on second reading that apparently every hon. member of the house intends to support this bill. I think it speaks well of the members who have taken part in the discussion and who have raised the level of debate to a constructive level that they have done a good deal to leave a very good taste in the mouths of those of us who have been somewhat responsible for bringing the bill forward to this stage.

As I listened to the debate there seemed to be three main questions, and at this time of night I do not intend to deal with them exhaustively. I will just mention them. The first question was: is a new minister required? I think I am quite prepared on the basis of my experience during the last two and a half years to say, yes, a minister is required. The house may not know it, but the act which sets out the responsibility of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources says that everything which does not belong to another minister belongs to the minister of northern affairs. If I had more time I should like to remind the house of other fields over which the act gives the department jurisdiction, quite apart from this matter of forestry, in connection with which there is so much to be done and so few hours of each day in which to do it.
The second question raised dealt with provincial rights. In view of the clear wording of the British North America Act, this is evidently a matter of proper consideration. I think the best test that can be afforded of the government's purpose in this regard is to compare the new bill with the act which the house is being asked to repeal. Clause 17 of the new bill asks parliament to repeal the Canada Forestry Act and if hon. members will compare the terms of that act with the operative clauses of this bill they will see clear signs that this bill is deliberately and carefully designed to ensure that there shall be no infringement of the rights of the provinces.
I was a little sorry tonight to hear the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) attack the provisions of this bill, particularly the subclauses in clause 9. Apparently the hon. member did not realize that he was criticizing provisions which were copied exactly from the Canada Forestry Act which does not make as clear as this bill does the distinction between the provincial and the federal fields. The Canada Forestry Act has no such provision for distinguishing clearly between these two fields. I think the young hon. member can only be excused because he did not do his homework and did not know sufficient about these measures to go and read their terms. The words he criticized tonight are taken out of the Canada Forestry Act which can be examined to ensure that I speak according to the facts. I do not think the hon. member did it deliberately, because we in a democratic country have a respect for those men who rise to the position of premier.
This act was passed under the guidance of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, who was minister of the crown in 1949. I do
Forestry Department
not think the hon. member for Lapointe intended to do injustice to the minister who held the portfolio before the change of government, the Hon. Mr. Lesage. Here is an act which was passed by Mr. St. Laurent and administered by Mr. Lesage, and yet attacked by the hon. member for Lapointe. I think if he compares the two he will see that this government did make clear-cut efforts to try and make sure that those who discussed this bill and those who are concerned with it will see that the jurisdiction of it is clearly limited in all cases to those lands belonging to Her Majesty in the right of Canada. Clause 5 refers to all matters over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction relating to the forestry resources of the country. We have clear-cut clauses to make that point very clear.
The final point that came up in the debate today was the growing number of hon. members who are aware of the broader use of the word "conservation". Conservation does not mean just simply saving something; it means the multiple use of those resources. These forests are just as useful, and will be increasingly useful in the field of agriculture as they are to the plain and straightforward interest of forestry.
Recreation has been mentioned. You could also point out that the trees have a great influence not only on the power resources of this country but also on the recreation and the fisheries resources, and so on. I would like to speak at length on this particular aspect of the question because this will be the measure of success of the new ministry. If it can bring to this country at every level, provincial, industrial and right down to the rank and file of the people of Canada just what it means to protect those forests in the real sense of the word, not only against fire, not only against pests and insects, not only against the depradations of humans who exploit them, but against dangers of the future, and think of their positive reason and the positive asset they are to this nation. If these things are recognized by people at all levels, then the real meaning of conservation in its broadest sense will be fully accepted.
Therefore, I want to express my own personal thanks to all hon. members of the house who have been so kind today, not only to me personally and to the government in general on having brought this bill forward but also because they put forward so many constructive ideas. In particular I should like to mention the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). Hon. members may not have noticed it, but this hon. member made a suggestion today that I predict that in the not so distant future will

Forestry Department
be a good measure of success of achieving this adjustment from a single type of resource development to a combined type of resource development, and particularly in relationship to agriculture and the forests.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Flynn in the chair.
Clauses 1 to 3, inclusive, agreed to.
On clause 4-Deputy Minister.

Subclause 2 of clause 4 pertains to administration of the departmental staff. It transfers staff from the Department of Agriculture and from the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Can the minister tell me whether or not the staff and the forestry officers coming under the northern administration branch of the Northwest Territories will be transferred to this new department?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: The northern affairs national resources section will keep those officers necessary to the administration of the resources of this area. We look on the territories as provinces to be, and we set up all our organizations there so that if ever a province is formed it will have all the officers it needs for various resources; therefore the various forestry officers who deal with administration of resources in the Yukon and Northwest Territories will stay with the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
Will this new forestry department control and make regulations in regard to the timber in the Wood Buffalo park?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, that comes under the National Parks Act.
All the wood cutting operations and operations in the park at the present time then come under the National Parks Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: That is right.
Can the minister give any indication as to how many people will be transferred from his department and from the Department of Agriculture to the new department?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I can give only an approximation at the moment, but one of my officials is coming down with the precise number. Maybe we can go on to another clause and revert to this clause later.

Perhaps I can ask the minister a question on this clause. Naturally he might not have at his disposal the number
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1
of officials to be transferred. Can he tell the committee what will be the research activities of the Department of Agriculture which will be taken over by the new department?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: The sections in agriculture in the biology section which deal with pests and forest diseases. There is the entomological section and the pathological section, and so on. Those sections which deal precisely with the forests will come over to the new department; but the institutes for the various scientific disciplines in agriculture will remain there. Three or four of the scientific disciplines are set up around an institute and each branch has various subsections. The one dealing with forest biology will move into the new department but will maintain very close liaison with those basic institutes of the various scientific disciplines.

I think this is the proper clause on which to ask this question. Will the new department take over responsibility for international work in the field of forestry? I am thinking of FAO work and commonwealth co-operation on forestry matters. I think there is a commonwealth forestry institute.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I think one of the clauses in the bill makes it clear that all the duties now carried out by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources forestry branch, and the duties carried out by the forest biological division of the Department of Agriculture, all those powers, all those contracts will be transferred to the new department, and anything dealing with the interest we have in world associations such as one meeting next month in Seattle will be under the new department.
What clause is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
The one I was
looking at was clause 14.

Before we leave this clause, the minister stated a moment ago that the wood cutting and timber operations in Wood Buffalo park come under the National Parks Act, Under northern affairs administration there are forestry officers who look after forestry within Wood Buffalo park, which is not a part of the Northwest Territories and therefore these men are not territorial staff. Are the forestry officials or any of them who are looking after Wood Buffalo park going to be transferred to the new department? They come under the Northwest Territories administration, not under national parks.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: The information I gave earlier is still true, that those forestry officers who deal with the administration of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon will remain under northern administration. On clause 6-Further duties.

I have a few questions on this clause. Subclause 1 (c) says that the minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, enter into agreements with the government of any province or with any person for forest protection and so on. speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
An example of that would be a contract with the pulp and paper research institute of Canada to do certain research work. Clause 5 as the operative clause makes it very clear, of course, that these are the duties, powers and functions of the minister. Clause 6 which we are discussing now outlines these duties in detail. The question has been raised whether these subclauses make it clear that there is no interference with provincial governments. I think that point could be resolved legally in a very simple way by saying that clause 5 is the governing clause with respect to the duties, powers and functions of the minister, but nevertheless I have with me an amendment which I am going to ask my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce to move.

6. (1) Subject to section 5, the minister

Forestry Department

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 6 as amended carry?

subtopic: HEALTH INSURANCE RATE REVISIONS
HEALTH INSURANCE RATE REVISIONS
speechtext:
1.	What consultation with or intimation to the federal government precedes an increase in hospitalization contributions required to be made to a province by families or individuals under the provisions of the hospital insurance and diagnostic act, and what controls, if any, on such contributions are available to the federal government?
2.	Since January 1, 1959, what provinces, if any, (a) have made upward revisions of rates; (b) have given notice to the federal government of an intention to increase rates of contributions by individuals, and what are the particulars of such prospective rate revisions?
Answer by: Hon. J. W. Monieilh (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
1.	No consultation with or intimation to the federal government precedes an increase in premium rates in those provinces operating hospital insurance programs on a premium basis.
Since the method by which a province raises its share of costs is the sole prerogative of the province, no controls on such premiums
Questions
are imposed by the federal government. There are however controls on the amount of co-insurance or deterrent charges levied by the provinces on insured persons for insured services, through the requirements that such charges must be described in the agreement with the federal government.
2.	Since January 1, 1959, Manitoba is the only province which has made an upward revision of premium rates (from $4.10 and $2.05 monthly to $6 and $3 monthly for families and single subscribers respectively).
The federal government has not been given any notice of an intention to increase rates of premiums for the reasons stated above.
